subject: humanities
passage: The earliest photographic processes, introduced in the late 1830s, required exposures that could last several minutes. During that time, anything that moved through the scene, such as a walking person or a passing carriage, left too little light in any one spot to register, whereas anything that held still was recorded sharply. Several early views of city boulevards known to have been crowded during the day show almost no one, apart from the occasional figure who happened to stay in place, such as a man standing still while his boots were polished. Viewers who conclude from such images that the boulevards were nearly empty are therefore most likely ______
stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: mistaking a limitation of the process for a feature of the scene.
choices.B: correct, since the photographs recorded everything within the frame.
choices.C: wrong to trust any image produced by the photographic processes of the 1830s.
choices.D: overlooking crowds that the photographers later scraped off the plates.

explanation.why: The long exposure meant that moving people left no image, while still figures did. The boulevards were known to be crowded, so their emptiness in the photographs comes from the process, not from the streets themselves.
explanation.A: Correct. Moving crowds did not register during the long exposures, so the empty look of the boulevards reflects how the process worked rather than what was there.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says the opposite: moving people and carriages did not register, so the photographs did not record everything in the frame.
explanation.C: Incorrect. Still objects, such as buildings and the man having his boots polished, were recorded sharply, so the images are not worthless.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text gives exposure time, not any retouching by photographers, as the reason crowds are missing.
